5. 
Notice of Issues and Alternatives. Unlike formal rulemaking or civil 
court proceedings, the procedures outUned in section 553 do not provide 
obvious opportunities for identifying contested issues of fact or policy that sin 
agency must resolve in framing final regulations. Agency notices of proposed 
rulemaking (NPRMs) typically describe the problem that proposed rules are 
intended to address, set forth a contemplated regulatory text, and specify 
issues on which comment is particularly invited. Even so, an agency’s notice 
may treat its premises only briefly and may fail to discuss alternative 
approaches. Further reflection may surface new issues within the agency, or 
thoughtful comments may advance new solutions. When the agency is 
persuaded to depart from its proposed solution, it may confront claims that its 
original notice did not adequately describe the options it was considering.
Following the consensus view that had developed in the lower courts since 
the 1970s, the Supreme Court has held that, in order for notice to be adequate 
under APA section 553, “the final rule the agency adopts must be a logical 
outgrowth of the rule proposed.” Long Island Care at Home, Ltd. v. Coke, 551 
U.S. 158, 174 (2007).
Note how this ‘logical outgrowth” doctrine can place the agency in a 
double bind. On the one hand, as we have seen, the arbitrary-or-capricious 
standard says courts will strike down a rulemaking if the agency fails to 
consider all important aspects of the matter, including if it fails to respond to 
every significant comment. On the other hand, the logical-outgrowth doctrine 
says courts will strike down a rulemaking if the agency is too responsive to the 
comments it receives, in the sense of actually changing the rule in response to 
them.
As an example of the logical outgrowth test’s appfication, consider a case 
that divided a panel of the Fifth Circuit, Mock v. Garland, 75 F.4th 563 (5th 
Cir. 2023). The National Firearms Act (NFA) and the Gun Control Act (GCA) 
“impose heightened, and at times, onerous requirements on manufacturing, 
selling, and transferring certain firearms, including short-barreled rifles 
(SBRs).” The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms (ATF) confronted the 
question of whether a “stabilizing brace, when attached to a pistol, transformed 
the pistol into a rifle and thus an SBR.” The agency issued an NPRM 
“indicating that the agency would use a point system to classify a firearm with 
a stabilizing brace as either a braced pistol or a rifle.” After receiving a tsunami
